facts.fact: On international care labels, dots inside the washtub symbol show the highest safe water temperature: one dot means 30 degrees Celsius, two dots 40, and three dots 50.
facts.hook: a teenager about to wash a new sweater on hot stops to count the dots on its label

facts.fact: On a care label, an empty triangle means any bleach may be used, while a triangle with a cross through it means the garment must not be bleached.
facts.hook: a kid reaches for the bleach to whiten a striped shirt and spots the crossed-out triangle just in time

facts.fact: Dots on the iron symbol set the highest safe iron setting: one dot is low, about 110 degrees Celsius, two is medium, about 150, and three is high, about 200.
facts.hook: a nylon costume shirt goes shiny under an iron left on the cotton setting

facts.fact: Laundry is sorted by colour because new dark or bright clothes can release dye into the wash water, and that dye can tint white and pale clothes.
facts.hook: a white school shirt comes out pink after sharing a load with one new red sock

facts.fact: Wool shrinks in hot, sloshing water because tiny scales on each wool fibre open up and lock onto neighbouring fibres, pulling the knit tighter. This is called felting.
facts.hook: a grandparent's hand-knitted sweater comes out of a hot wash small enough for a doll

facts.fact: A blood stain should be rinsed in cold water, because hot water makes the proteins in blood set into the fabric fibres and much harder to remove.
facts.hook: after a nosebleed on a borrowed shirt, a kid has to decide between the hot tap and the cold one

facts.fact: High-efficiency washing machines need low-sudsing HE detergent; regular detergent makes too many suds in their small amount of water, cushioning the clothes and leaving soap residue.
facts.hook: foam creeps out of the door of a friend's new washer after the wrong detergent goes in

facts.fact: Detergent molecules have one end that is attracted to water and another end that is attracted to oil and grease, so they lift greasy dirt off fabric into the wash water.
facts.hook: a pizza-grease stain that water alone would not shift finally lifts out with detergent

facts.fact: Chlorine bleach must never be mixed with cleaners containing ammonia, because together they release chloramine, a toxic gas.
facts.hook: a kid helping with a big clean reads both bottle labels and stops before pouring one into the other

facts.fact: According to the U.S. Fire Administration, failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires, because built-up lint blocks the airflow and lets heat collect.
facts.hook: a thick grey mat of lint in the dryer filter turns out to be a job nobody has been doing

facts.fact: A paper tissue left in a pocket breaks apart in the wash and scatters white shreds over every item in the load, which is why pockets are checked before washing.
facts.hook: a whole load of dark clothes comes out speckled white from one forgotten tissue

facts.fact: Clothes left crumpled in a dryer or basket after the cycle ends tend to wrinkle as they cool, so taking them out promptly and folding them helps keep them smooth.
facts.hook: a shirt left in the dryer overnight comes out creased on the morning of a job interview for a sibling

facts.fact: In F. Scott Fitzgerald's novel The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, a green light glows at the end of Daisy Buchanan's dock, across the water from Gatsby's house.
facts.hook: a book club member notices Gatsby reaching toward a light on the very first night of the story

facts.fact: Readers usually take The Great Gatsby's green light to stand for Gatsby's hope of winning Daisy, and by the novel's end for a dream that cannot be reached, however rich he becomes.
facts.hook: two friends argue over whether the green light means the same thing in chapter one and the last chapter

facts.fact: In William Golding's Lord of the Flies, published in 1954, Ralph blows a conch shell like a horn to gather the stranded boys, and the shell becomes a sign of order and fair meetings.
facts.hook: a student marks every page where someone holds the conch and sees who gets to speak

facts.fact: In Lord of the Flies, the conch is smashed at the same moment Piggy is killed, which readers take as the final collapse of order among the boys.
facts.hook: a reader realizes the conch and Piggy disappear from the story together

facts.fact: In Lord of the Flies, Piggy's glasses are first used to light the boys' signal fire for rescue, and later Jack's tribe steals them in the night.
facts.hook: a student's chart shows the glasses changing hands from rescue to raid

facts.fact: In Lord of the Flies, the beast the boys fear on the mountain turns out to be the body of a dead airman under a parachute, which they mistake for a monster.
facts.hook: a reader rereads the mountain scene after learning what the shape really was

facts.fact: In Lord of the Flies, Simon comes to understand that the beast is not a creature on the island but something inside the boys themselves.
facts.hook: a book club discussion turns when someone asks whether the beast was ever real

facts.fact: In Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter, published in 1850, Hester Prynne's scarlet A begins as a mark of shame, but years later many townspeople say it stands for Able.
facts.hook: a student tracks what the letter A means to the town at the start and near the end

facts.fact: In Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird, published in 1960, Miss Maudie explains that it is a sin to kill a mockingbird because mockingbirds do nothing but sing their hearts out for us.
facts.hook: a reader starts listing which characters in the book are like mockingbirds

facts.fact: In Suzanne Collins's The Hunger Games, published in 2008, Madge Undersee gives Katniss a mockingjay pin before Katniss goes into the arena.
facts.hook: a reader wonders why a small gift in chapter one matters so much by the end of the series

facts.fact: In The Hunger Games, mockingjays were never planned by the Capitol: they came from its engineered jabberjay birds breeding with wild female mockingbirds.
facts.hook: a book club member argues that the bird already means something before Katniss ever wears it

facts.fact: A motif is an image, object or idea that keeps recurring through a literary work, and tracking where it reappears helps a reader see what it comes to mean.
facts.hook: a student keeps sticky notes on every page where a certain object shows up

facts.fact: In Shakespeare's English, wherefore means why, so Juliet's line "Wherefore art thou Romeo?" asks why he has to be Romeo, not where he is.
facts.hook: a student's paraphrase says Juliet is looking for Romeo, and a classmate checks the word

facts.fact: In Shakespeare's time, thou was used for close friends, family or people of lower rank, and sometimes as an insult, while you was the polite form for superiors and strangers.
facts.hook: a reader notices a character suddenly switching from you to thou in the middle of an argument

facts.fact: In Shakespeare's English, thee is the object form of thou, the way me is the object form of I, so "I love thee" means "I love you".
facts.hook: a student paraphrasing a speech gets stuck on why the word keeps changing between thou and thee

facts.fact: In Shakespeare's English, verbs used with thou usually end in -est, so "thou knowest" means "you know".
facts.hook: a reader stumbles over a line full of -est words until the pattern clicks

facts.fact: In Shakespeare's English, he or she verbs often end in -eth or -th, so doth means does and hath means has.
facts.hook: a paraphrase group turns "she hath" into plain modern English

facts.fact: In Shakespeare's English, anon means at once or soon, so a servant calling "Anon!" is saying "Coming right away!"
facts.hook: a class reads a scene where a servant keeps shouting the same odd word at the door

facts.fact: Prithee is a squeezed-together form of "I pray thee" and means please.
facts.hook: a student realizes a character who says prithee is being polite, not strange

facts.fact: In Shakespeare's English, a line beginning "Would that" expresses a wish, so "Would that it were so" means "I wish it were so".
facts.hook: a reader misreads a wish as a question until someone explains the old use of would

facts.fact: Shakespeare wrote much of his verse in iambic pentameter: lines of about ten syllables in five pairs, each an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one.
facts.hook: a class taps out the beat of a speech on their desks, da-DUM five times

facts.fact: Shakespeare often gave verse to nobles and prose to servants and comic characters, though not always, so a switch between them can signal a change in mood or rank.
facts.hook: a reader notices the lines stop looking like poetry when the servants start talking

facts.fact: A soliloquy is a speech in which a character, usually alone on stage, speaks their private thoughts aloud so the audience can hear them.
facts.hook: a student paraphrasing a soliloquy realizes the character is telling the audience a secret

facts.fact: The stage direction exit is Latin for "he or she goes out," and exeunt is Latin for "they go out," used when two or more characters leave.
facts.hook: a reader wonders why the script says exeunt at the end of a crowded scene

facts.fact: A topic is a subject a novel is about, such as friendship, while a theme is a full statement of what the novel says about that subject.
facts.hook: a student writes "the theme is friendship" and a book club friend asks what the book says about it

facts.fact: A novel's theme is usually implied rather than stated outright, so readers infer it from what the characters do and what happens to them.
facts.hook: a reader searches the book for a sentence that says the moral and cannot find one

facts.fact: Novels commonly have more than one theme, so two readers can name different themes for the same book and both support them with evidence.
facts.hook: two friends at a book club each defend a different theme for the same novel

facts.fact: A theme is usually written about people in general rather than one character, so it could apply to readers' lives outside the book.
facts.hook: a student rewrites "Auggie learns to be brave" into something anyone could learn

facts.fact: A quotation used as evidence must be copied word for word, with the same spelling and punctuation, inside quotation marks.
facts.hook: a student quotes a line from memory, then checks the page and finds two words were wrong

facts.fact: In MLA style, three spaced periods, called an ellipsis, show where words have been left out of the middle of a quotation.
facts.hook: a quotation is too long for a paragraph, so a student trims the middle and has to show it

facts.fact: In MLA style, square brackets go around any word a writer adds to a quotation, to show it was not in the original text.
facts.hook: a quote says "he" and a student needs to make clear which character that means

facts.fact: In MLA style, an in-text citation for a novel gives the author's last name and the page number in parentheses, with no comma between them.
facts.hook: a teacher's note says the essay's quotes need page numbers the reader can check

facts.fact: In MLA style, a prose quotation longer than four lines is set as an indented block, half an inch from the margin, without quotation marks.
facts.hook: a student's favourite passage is too long to fit inside a sentence

facts.fact: A character's words are not always the author's view, because a novel may show a character's opinion only to argue against it.
facts.hook: a student quotes a bully's line as the book's message and a friend points out who said it

facts.fact: In R. J. Palacio's novel Wonder, published in 2012, the teacher Mr. Browne gives the precept "When given the choice between being right or being kind, choose kind."
facts.hook: a reader picks the one quotation that best backs up the book's theme about kindness

facts.fact: In S. E. Hinton's The Outsiders, published in 1967, Johnny's dying message to Ponyboy is to "stay gold," meaning to hold on to his goodness and innocence.
facts.hook: a book club uses two short words from a letter to prove what the whole novel is about

facts.fact: Foreshadowing is a hint early in a story about something that will happen later, often noticed only on a second reading.
facts.hook: a reader finishing a short story flips back and finds the clue was there on page one

facts.fact: In letters starting in 1889, Anton Chekhov advised writers that a rifle shown hanging on the wall early in a play must go off later, or it should not be there.
facts.hook: a reader spots an object described in detail at the start and waits for it to matter

facts.fact: A red herring is a false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion, so not every hint in a story is real foreshadowing.
facts.hook: a book club is sure they know the ending, and the clue they trusted was a trap

facts.fact: Shirley Jackson's story The Lottery, published in The New Yorker in 1948, opens with children piling up stones, a detail that hints at how the lottery ends.
facts.hook: a class rereads the calm first paragraph after finishing the story and sees the stones differently

facts.fact: In W. W. Jacobs's 1902 story The Monkey's Paw, Sergeant-Major Morris warns that the paw's wishes bring terrible results and throws it into the fire before the family rescues it.
facts.hook: a reader argues that the story warned everyone before the first wish was made

facts.fact: In Richard Connell's 1924 story The Most Dangerous Game, the island's name, Ship-Trap Island, and sailors' fear of it hint at the danger waiting there.
facts.hook: a student notices that a place name gives away more than the characters realize

facts.fact: The Most Dangerous Game opens with the hunter Rainsford saying hunted animals have no feelings, which foreshadows him becoming the one who is hunted.
facts.hook: a reader realizes an early argument about jaguars sets up the whole ending

facts.fact: In James Hurst's 1960 story The Scarlet Ibis, a storm-blown red bird dies in the family garden, foreshadowing the fate of the fragile boy Doodle.
facts.hook: a reader connects a bird's death to what happens to a character a few pages later

facts.fact: In O. Henry's 1905 story The Gift of the Magi, Della sells her long hair to buy a chain for Jim's watch, while Jim sells his watch to buy combs for her hair.
facts.hook: a class debates whether the useless gifts show the couple lost or won

facts.fact: In Guy de Maupassant's 1884 story The Necklace, Mathilde spends ten years repaying a lost borrowed necklace, then learns the original was worthless costume jewellery.
facts.hook: a reader explains what the necklace stood for once the truth comes out

facts.fact: The critic John Ruskin coined the term pathetic fallacy in 1856 for giving nature human feelings, such as a sullen sky, which writers use to hint at a story's mood.
facts.hook: a student notices the weather turns stormy right before things go wrong in the story

facts.fact: A symbol is an object, person or event that stands for an idea beyond itself, and a reader must support any meaning they give it with details from the story.
facts.hook: a book club member claims a red door means danger and is asked to prove it from the text

facts.fact: The haka Ka Mate was composed around 1820 by the Ngāti Toa chief Te Rauparaha to celebrate surviving after hiding from enemies who were chasing him.
facts.hook: a student learning the haka for a school welcome asks what the words are celebrating

facts.fact: Hula kahiko, the older style of Hawaiian hula, is danced to chanting and traditional instruments such as gourd drums rather than to sung melodies.
facts.hook: a young dancer practising for a festival learns to keep time to a chant instead of a song

facts.fact: Hula ʻauana, the modern style of Hawaiian hula that grew up under Western influence, is danced to sung melodies with instruments such as guitar and ukulele.
facts.hook: a cousin shows the difference between two hula styles by switching the music

facts.fact: In the Philippine dance tinikling, two people tap bamboo poles on the ground twice and then clap them together on the third beat while dancers step in and out.
facts.hook: a nervous dancer keeps count out loud so their ankles stay clear of the closing poles

facts.fact: A Chinese lion dance is normally performed by two dancers inside one costume, one working the head and the other the tail, to drums, gongs and cymbals.
facts.hook: two friends practising the lion dance keep tripping until they learn to move as one

facts.fact: Bharatanatyam, a classical dance from Tamil Nadu in India, uses symbolic hand gestures called mudras that work like words to tell a story.
facts.hook: a student practising for a festival forgets one hand gesture and changes the meaning

facts.fact: A Bharatanatyam dancer's first full solo performance is called an arangetram, meaning ascending the stage, and marks the end of their first formal training.
facts.hook: an older cousin's arangetram inspires a younger dancer to keep practising

facts.fact: In traditional and competition Irish step dancing, dancers keep the upper body and arms held still while the feet do fast, intricate footwork.
facts.hook: a beginner's arms keep flapping until a teacher has them practise with hands pressed to their sides

facts.fact: Dabke is a Levantine line dance whose name comes from an Arabic word for stamping the feet; it is often danced at weddings, led by a skilled leader.
facts.hook: a kid at a family wedding is finally invited to join the line and must match the stamps

facts.fact: The jingle dress dance began among Ojibwe communities around 1900, and the dress's jingles were first made from tobacco can lids rolled into cones.
facts.hook: a young dancer and a grandparent roll cones for a new dress before a gathering

facts.fact: In call-and-response singing, a leader sings a line and the group answers; the pattern is deeply rooted in African musical traditions and in gospel and work songs.
facts.hook: a shy singer volunteers to lead the call at a community event

facts.fact: Learning spread over several short sessions is remembered better than the same amount crammed into one session, a finding called the spacing effect, first described by Hermann Ebbinghaus in 1885.
facts.hook: a kid who crammed a song the night before forgets the second verse on stage

facts.fact: In Hinduism, the soul passes through samsara, a cycle of birth, death and rebirth, and a person's karma, the results of their actions, shapes their next life.
facts.hook: a student compares notes with a Hindu friend at a family gathering after a grandparent's death

facts.fact: In Hinduism, moksha is liberation from the cycle of rebirth, and it is considered the highest goal of human life.
facts.hook: a kid asks a grandparent whether being reborn is something to hope for or to escape

facts.fact: Hindus usually cremate the dead, returning the body to the five elements, though young children and some holy people are traditionally buried instead.
facts.hook: a student notices two families at different ceremonies handle funerals very differently

facts.fact: Buddhism teaches rebirth but denies a permanent soul, called anatta or no-self, so what continues from life to life is a chain of karma, not an unchanging self.
facts.hook: two friends comparing Hindu and Buddhist beliefs discover a difference they had missed

facts.fact: In Buddhism, reaching nirvana ends the cycle of rebirth by ending the craving and ignorance that keep it going.
facts.hook: a student writes a comparison chart and has to explain how the cycle stops in each faith

facts.fact: Sikhism accepts rebirth and karma, but Guru Nanak taught that the body takes birth because of karma while salvation is attained through God's grace.
facts.hook: a Sikh classmate explains why good deeds alone are not the whole answer in her faith

facts.fact: In Islam, barzakh, an Arabic word for barrier, is the stage the soul passes through between a person's death and the resurrection.
facts.hook: a Muslim friend at a cemetery visit explains where her grandfather is now, according to her faith

facts.fact: Islam teaches that on the Day of Judgment, called Yawm al-Qiyamah, all people will be raised and judged, and sent to paradise or hell.
facts.hook: a comparison project puts one faith's single life and judgment beside another's many lives

facts.fact: The Catholic Church teaches purgatory, a state of purification after death before entering heaven, but most Protestant churches reject the idea.
facts.hook: two Christian friends are surprised to find their churches teach different things

facts.fact: The Nicene Creed, recited in many Christian churches, ends by looking forward to the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.
facts.hook: a student hears the creed at a funeral and asks what those final words mean

facts.fact: The Jewish afterlife is often called olam ha-ba, meaning the world to come, though the phrase itself does not appear in the Hebrew Bible.
facts.hook: a Jewish friend explains a Hebrew phrase heard at a shiva house

facts.fact: Jewish views of the afterlife vary widely: Orthodox Judaism holds to a future resurrection of the dead, while Reform Judaism puts more weight on how people live now.
facts.hook: two Jewish cousins from different synagogues give different answers to the same question

facts.fact: Shabbat, the Jewish day of rest, begins at sunset on Friday and ends after nightfall on Saturday.
facts.hook: a kid spending a Friday at a friend's house is surprised when the phones are put away at sunset

facts.fact: Havdalah, a Hebrew word meaning separation, is the ceremony that ends Shabbat on Saturday night once three stars can be seen in the sky.
facts.hook: a family's children race to the window to count the first three stars

facts.fact: The Havdalah ceremony uses a cup of wine or grape juice, fragrant spices to smell, and a braided candle with several wicks.
facts.hook: a younger sibling is allowed to hold the braided candle for the first time

facts.fact: In Islam, fasting during Ramadan is not required of children before puberty, so many younger children practise by fasting for part of a day.
facts.hook: an eleven-year-old tries fasting until lunchtime to be part of the family's Ramadan

facts.fact: Islam excuses people who are sick or travelling from the Ramadan fast, and they make up the missed days later.
facts.hook: a kid with a fever worries about missing the fast until a parent explains the rule

facts.fact: During Ramadan, Muslims eat a meal called suhur before the dawn prayer, then go without food and drink until sunset.
facts.hook: an alarm goes off before dawn and the whole family gathers sleepily in the kitchen

facts.fact: Many Muslims break their daily fast at sunset with dates and water, following the example of the Prophet Muhammad, before eating a larger meal called iftar.
facts.hook: a friend invited to iftar wonders why everyone reaches for dates first

facts.fact: The Yom Kippur fast lasts about 25 hours, from sunset one day until after nightfall the next.
facts.hook: a kid who wants to try the fast asks how long it really lasts

facts.fact: Jewish law waives the Yom Kippur fast when health is in danger, and in that case a person is actually required to eat or drink.
facts.hook: a diabetic cousin is told by the rabbi that eating is the religious thing to do

facts.fact: On Buddhist observance days called uposatha, devout lay Buddhists may take eight precepts, including not eating after midday.
facts.hook: a kid visits a temple with family and learns why no one is eating an afternoon snack

facts.fact: Ekadashi, the eleventh day of each half of the Hindu lunar month, is a fasting day dedicated to Vishnu on which many Hindus avoid grains and beans.
facts.hook: a kid wonders why a grandparent skips rice twice a month

facts.fact: Muslims perform the ritual prayer, salah, five times a day, facing the Kaaba in Mecca.
facts.hook: a Muslim student at a community hall uses a phone compass to find the right direction to pray

facts.fact: In Orthodox Judaism, boys become bar mitzvah at 13 and girls become bat mitzvah at 12, while most Reform and Conservative communities celebrate both at 13.
facts.hook: twin cousins at different synagogues have their ceremonies in different years

facts.fact: A Torah scroll is written without vowels or musical marks, so a bar or bat mitzvah student learns the chanted melody of their reading in advance from a printed book.
facts.hook: a student opens the real scroll at rehearsal and sees none of the marks from their practice book

facts.fact: A Torah reader follows the words with a yad, a pointer whose name means hand, so that the parchment itself is not touched.
facts.hook: a nervous student's finger drifts toward the scroll and a teacher hands over the pointer

facts.fact: At a bar or bat mitzvah, the young person often also chants the haftarah, a reading from the books of the Prophets.
facts.hook: a student realizes they have two readings to learn, not one

facts.fact: In the Hindu upanayana ceremony, a young person receives a sacred thread, and learning to recite the Gayatri Mantra marks the actual start of their initiation.
facts.hook: a boy practises the mantra with a grandparent every evening before his ceremony

facts.fact: The sacred thread given at upanayana is worn diagonally, over the left shoulder and under the right arm.
facts.hook: a kid putting on the thread for the first time gets it on the wrong shoulder

facts.fact: Japji Sahib, by Guru Nanak, opens the Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, has 38 stanzas called pauris, and is recited by devout Sikhs every morning.
facts.hook: a Sikh teenager sets a goal of reciting the morning prayer without looking

facts.fact: Japji Sahib is also recited at the Sikh Khalsa initiation ceremony, called Amrit Sanchar.
facts.hook: a young Sikh preparing for initiation learns why the morning prayer matters so much

facts.fact: A person who has memorized the entire Quran, all 114 chapters, is called a hafiz, and keeping it perfectly remembered takes constant practice.
facts.hook: a kid meets an older cousin who recites from memory what the kid is still learning

facts.fact: In Mexican tradition, a quinceañera, the celebration of a girl's fifteenth birthday, usually begins with a Mass of thanksgiving.
facts.hook: a girl preparing for her quinceañera has to learn a reading for the Mass

facts.fact: Testing yourself by reciting from memory helps you remember longer than rereading, a finding called the testing effect, shown by Roediger and Karpicke in 2006.
facts.hook: a student stops rereading a prayer and starts saying it aloud with the page face down

facts.fact: The method of loci is a memory trick of linking each part of a text to a place along a familiar route, then walking that route in your mind to recall it.
facts.hook: a kid memorizes each line of a reading by placing it in a different room of a grandparent's house

facts.fact: In Spanish, a la derecha means to the right, but derecho, as in sigue derecho, means keep going straight, and learners often confuse the two.
facts.hook: a traveller turns right after being told to go straight on

facts.fact: In French, à droite means to the right, while tout droit means straight ahead, a pair that often trips up learners asking for directions.
facts.hook: a student on a school trip turns right when the passer-by meant straight ahead

facts.fact: In German, links means left, rechts means right, and geradeaus means straight ahead.
facts.hook: a kid at a language class practises by guiding a blindfolded friend around the room

facts.fact: In Spanish, the question "¿Dónde está...?" means "Where is...?", and adding "por favor" makes it polite.
facts.hook: a student at a cultural festival needs to find the bathroom and has only one phrase ready

facts.fact: In Spanish, a la izquierda means to the left, so la primera calle a la izquierda means the first street on the left.
facts.hook: a learner repeats the directions back to check which street to take

facts.fact: In much of Latin America, a cuadra is a city block, so directions like dos cuadras mean two blocks.
facts.hook: a traveller counts streets instead of blocks and walks past the place

facts.fact: When asking a stranger for directions, Spanish speakers usually use the polite usted, French speakers vous, and German speakers Sie, rather than the familiar form.
facts.hook: a student asks an older woman for directions and catches their too-casual pronoun

facts.fact: In Spanish, "Más despacio, por favor" means "More slowly, please," a phrase that helps learners follow a fast answer.
facts.hook: a passer-by's directions come too fast until the student asks them to slow down

facts.fact: In French, "Excusez-moi" is used to get a stranger's attention politely before asking a question, and "s'il vous plaît" means please.
facts.hook: a learner practising at home rehearses how to stop someone on the street politely

facts.fact: In Mandarin Chinese, zuǒ means left and yòu means right, each said with its own tone.
facts.hook: a grandparent teaches a kid the two direction words while walking to the market

facts.fact: Street names are rarely used in Japanese addresses outside a few cities such as Kyoto, so people giving directions usually point to landmarks and train stations.
facts.hook: a student asks for a street name in Japanese and gets directions by landmarks instead

facts.fact: Language learners can usually understand more words than they can say, so a learner may follow spoken directions they could not yet give themselves.
facts.hook: a kid who could barely ask the question understands most of the answer
